section: Results: Changing the Model Instead of the Labels
text: This shows that the ranking of noise-handling methods changes with the feature space, so a ranking made on one representation does not carry to another.
Cleaning keeps the hybrid ahead on small molecules.
Before any treatment the hybrid already beats the best single representation in almost every small-molecule condition, and after mitigation it still does.
On LogD with outliers, for example, the network's cleaned hybrid scores 0.5560 against 0.5915 for the cleaned single representation.
Cleaning rarely changes which of the two wins, and when it does it more often moves the win to the hybrid.
On antibodies the hybrid is ahead in about half the conditions, before and after cleaning, so there is no lead to keep.
The reaction set sits between the two.
The closest test of the question this thesis started from, whether a better feature set makes noise handling work, is where the detector finds its neighbors.
One experiment down-weights molecules by the neighbor gap and finds the neighbors either in the model's own single representation or in the hybrid, with everything else held fixed.
Finding them in the hybrid helped the same model on the same single representation slightly more often.
The largest differences go both ways.
On LogD under a scaffold-family shift, the network's single representation goes from 0.7051 to 0.6626 RMSE with neighbors in the hybrid, and gets worse with neighbors in its own space.
On antibody thermostability with outliers, the network barely moves with its own neighbors and gains with the hybrid's.
On expression titer under Gaussian noise the reverse happens, and its own neighbors help more than the hybrid's.
These are the largest cases picked out of many, not typical ones.
No control has run for this comparison.
The network gains from cleaning more often than the support vector regressor on Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD.
Part of that may be the network's own spread between fits, since a deterministic model with an unchanged score never counts as helped.
On binding free energy the support vector regressor gains more often, and on expression titer the random forest gains more often than the network.
Noise mitigation works in QSAR data, and it works best when something other than a model tells us which labels are wrong.
A clipped label is flagged by the assay limit, and a shifted scaffold family by its scaffold.
In both cases moving the flagged labels won back about half or more of the lost RMSE on every small-molecule dataset where the damage hurt.
When a detector has to infer which labels are wrong, mitigation still helped.
Under hERG's label flips it beat random deletion on three folds.
But the gains were smaller, and they depended on whether the detector's precision cleared the break-even point for that damage.
Under outliers the forest residual's precision was well above it.
Under shifts in a few labels it was well below it, and acting on its flags did little.
Chapter [REF] found that no model's own uncertainty picks out the corrupted labels, and that models are most certain about the labels that were clipped.
This chapter agrees from the other side.
The residual detector fell to chance under censoring, because a model fitted to clipped labels predicts the clipped values.
The three detectors that predict a spread from the features alone could not be graded at all, because they never read a label.
And the damage that was most fixable is the damage that needs no detector.
For the labels as delivered there is no truth to grade against, so a gain can come from removing hard molecules rather than wrong ones.
The shuffled-score control separates the two.
On small molecules it leaves one clear result, label smoothing on hERG K_i, and small gains on Caco-2 and LogD.
On three antibody sets, SMAC colloidal stability, binding free energy and expression titer, cleaning passes the control, on SMAC by a wide margin.
We read that as real, with the caution that each held-out fold has only about 50 antibodies.
Cleaning an experimental dataset with nothing injected is a use case in its own right, and on those three datasets it is the one that paid off most.
Was fixing the feature set the right place to start?
On small molecules the hybrid started ahead, and it stays ahead through every kind of cleaning, so a user who builds a hybrid loses nothing by cleaning afterwards.
The detectors told a more mixed story.
Neighbors found in the hybrid led to better cleaning slightly more often than neighbors in a single representation.
For detection alone, though, the importance-weighted features of a single representation did better than the hybrid's.
The hybrid search itself turned out to be robust to Gaussian noise: searching on damaged labels instead of clean ones changed Caco-2's score in the third decimal.
And the ranking of noise-handling methods changed between the hybrid and the single representations in almost every condition.
That is the result that ties this chapter to Chapter [REF].
A noise-handling method is not good or bad on its own.
It is good or bad in a feature space.
Most results rest on the first outer fold.

Further folds exist for the clipped-label corrections on LogD and Caco-2, deletion under hERG's flips, label smoothing and cliff put-back on hERG K_i, and the comparison of searches on clean and damaged labels.
They mostly agree with fold 0, and the text gives the exceptions.
The results to confirm on all folds first are, in order:
SMAC colloidal stability, deletion and relabeling on the labels as delivered.
hERG K_i, relabeling and putting cliff molecules back.
hERG, deletion and relabeling under the flip kinds.
The clipped-label corrections.
The scaffold-family offsets.
Most methods have no control.
Six controls ran, one per experiment (Section [REF]), and none on an antibody dataset under injected damage.
The random put-back control was usable only on hERG K_i.
Three of the methods with large gains have no QM9 result with no noise added: changing the model, cleaning before the search, and moving every label toward a Huber-fitted prediction.
Until those exist, their gains cannot be split into noise removed and a better model.
QM9 is our only clean control, and we tested one of its properties, the HOMO--LUMO gap.
A control on more computed properties would show whether the QM9 results hold beyond that one target.
There is also no way to correct a label without ground truth and know it was corrected, and no dataset here has a measured floor of assay error below which no model can go.
Seven of the datasets in Chapters [REF] and [REF] have no noise results yet: adme\_mdr1, adme\_rlm, flab\_expression\_koenig, flab\_binding\_koenig, abagym\_EGFR, abagym\_Ang2 and ginkgo\_hic.
Noisy labels in QSAR data can be found and, under the right conditions, fixed.
Fixing works best with a flag: raising labels clipped at an assay limit won back half to three quarters of the lost RMSE on the small-molecule datasets, and needed no detector.
With a detector, deleting or relabeling flagged molecules helped under label flips and outliers, and passed random and shuffled controls on hERG, hERG K_i, Buchwald--Hartwig and three antibody sets.
On clean QM9 labels deletion never helped, so those gains are noise removed.
The hybrid stays ahead of the single representation on small molecules through every treatment, and the ranking of noise-handling methods depends on the feature space they run in.
Chapter [REF] brings these results together with the rest of the thesis.
Chapter [REF] asked what makes a QSAR model robust to label noise.
Model family was the main factor in noise robustness, while the representation mattered more for predictive performance than for robustness.
Grouped-shifted noise and censoring, the two conditions where the error is systematic, did the most damage.
The shape of the noise distribution made little difference.
Random forests were the most consistent model across the four datasets.
Mean predicted uncertainty rose with noise, but no model's uncertainty for a single molecule picked out which labels had been corrupted.
Under censoring the models were most confident about the clipped labels.
Chapter [REF] looked at why the published methods for learning with noisy labels did so poorly in that setting.
On a single dataset, very little of a standard representation varies.
On hERG K_i, 1,815 of the 2,048 ECFP4 features take one value in at least 95\% of the molecules, and 56 of the 1,412 molecules share their feature vector with another molecule.
A distance sums over every feature, so the features that carry nothing dominate it.
Methods that judge a label by its neighbors' labels inherit this, and in the exploratory study they usually made the model worse.
Chapter [REF] built the adaptive hybrid representation.
A search selects features from up to ten base representations for one dataset and downstream model, inside each fold.
On every small-molecule dataset the hybrid beat the best single representation with both downstream models, and on the six regression datasets it did so on every fold.
On LogD with the SVM it went from 0.4930 to 0.4302 RMSE, and on QM9 with the DNN from 0.3619 to 0.3155 eV.
It also beat the single representation that was best in hindsight, which no user could pick in advance.
On antibodies the gains depend on the dataset.
On the anti-VEGF expression scan the hybrid went from 0.7029 to 0.7729 Spearman with the SVM, ahead on all five folds, and on binding free energy from 0.1317 to 0.3542 with the DNN.
Chapter [REF] asked whether a hybrid built for distance gives better neighbors.
On all five small-molecule datasets it does.
On hERG K_i the correlation between the distance of two molecules and the difference in their activity goes from 0.0729 to 0.2625 Spearman.
Predicting each molecule from its five nearest neighbors goes from 0.6280 to 0.5822 RMSE.
On the antibody datasets and the Buchwald--Hartwig reactions distance also tracks activity more closely, but prediction from neighbors is worse in the hybrid on several of them.
Chapter [REF] returned to label noise, with the single representation and the hybrid side by side.
Noise mitigation works.
With a quarter of LogD's training labels clipped at an assay limit, censored EM took the network from 0.6354 to 0.4795 RMSE, against 0.4314 before clipping.
Under hERG's label flips, deleting the flagged molecules took gradient-boosted trees on the hybrid from 0.8028 to 0.8375 AUROC, against 0.8179 for random deletion of the same size.
On the labels as delivered, label smoothing took the network on hERG K_i from 0.6380 to 0.5775 RMSE, where shuffled detector scores stayed at 0.6419 or above.
On SMAC colloidal stability, deleting the flagged antibodies took the SVM from 0.2740 to 0.4034 Spearman, against at most 0.2782 with shuffled scores.
There is no single best model, representation, similarity measure, method for learning with noisy labels or noise mitigation method that fits every dataset.
Everything depends on the data: the features, the true labels, and the noise those labels carry.
Every dataset carries its own noise, as outliers and activity cliffs, and it is not predictable in advance.
So the honest answer is not a winner.
It is a broad sweep, which this thesis runs again and again, together with hybrid featurization, a procedure that builds a feature selection for each dataset.
The hybrid is not a one-size-fits-all method.
It adapts to the data it is given, including data whose corruption is unknown, and it adapts further when used alongside noise mitigation.
The claim is not ``this method works''.
It is that no single method can work, so we should change the data, in terms of its features, instead.
The hybrid builds a different selection for each dataset and model, and this is what the search is for.
On Caco-2 it picked 1,000 to 2,000 features for the DNN on every fold, and 500 to 1,000 for the SVM.
Most small-molecule folds drew on all ten representations, while the Buchwald--Hartwig searches drew on two on every fold, and QM9 with LightGBM on three.
Across the configurations of one search, the downstream model accounted for 48.5\% of the variance in score on LogD and the budget for 1.4\%.
A fixed recipe would have to get all of these right at once, for every dataset.
The hybrid and noise mitigation also work together.
Because the hybrid's features are chosen against the labels, the labels can be cleaned before the search instead of after it.
On the expression titer labels as delivered, the network on the hybrid scores 0.1550 Spearman with no cleaning.
Deleting the antibodies the forest residual flags raises it to 0.3899 when only the fit sees the cleaned labels, and to 0.5619 when the search sees them too.
The hybrid can also be the space in which a detector finds its neighbors.

On LogD under a scaffold-family shift, down-weighting by the neighbor gap took the network's single representation from 0.7051 RMSE to 0.7535 with neighbors in its own space, and to 0.6626 with neighbors in the hybrid.
Both results are on one fold, and neither has a control yet, but they are what ``adapts further alongside noise mitigation'' looks like in practice.

text: This is what lets the thesis say that a gain is noise removed, and not just a model that got lucky.
The strongest noise results in this thesis came where something other than a model says which labels are wrong.
A clipped label is flagged by the assay limit itself.
The correction then only has to decide how far to raise it, and no detector is needed.
With a quarter of LogD's training labels clipped, censored EM won back 76\% of the RMSE that clipping cost the network, and on the hybrid it went from 0.6049 to 0.4610.
The gain held on each of the four folds where it was run.
On QM9, where the labels before clipping carry no assay error, LightGBM on the hybrid went from 0.5240 to 0.4301 against 0.3694 before clipping.
Knowing which labels are clipped is what helps.
Knowing how far each one should go is not.
Raising each clipped label by its own estimated amount did worse than dealing the same amounts to the wrong clipped molecules.
For the network on LogD's hybrid it gave 0.4988 RMSE, against 0.4714, 0.4673 and 0.4632 with the amounts shuffled.
Deleting the clipped molecules, which uses the same flag but throws them away, was the worst choice of all, because the model then never sees a high label.
Scaffold families behave the same way when each carries its own offset.
The family is the flag, and subtracting each family's estimated offset took the network on Caco-2's hybrid from 0.3214 to 0.2796 RMSE on the first damaged draw, against 0.2385 on clean labels.
When a detector has to infer which labels are wrong, mitigation still helps, but less, and only when the detector is precise enough.
Under outliers, the forest residual's top 5\% are mostly damaged molecules, and acting on them pays off.
On hERG K_i with outliers, down-weighting the flagged molecules took the network on the hybrid from 0.6917 to 0.6388 RMSE, while down-weighting the same number of undamaged molecules made it worse.
Under a shift in a few labels the residual's precision stayed below the point where acting on it pays off.
And deletion never helped on clean labels.
On QM9 with no noise added, the best deletion took the network's hybrid from 0.3550 to 0.3931 RMSE.
So where deletion helps on damaged labels and beats random deletion, the gain is noise removed.
Every clipped-label result above is on injected clipping, where the limit is known.
CHO polyreactivity is the one dataset in this thesis with a floor visible in its labels, with 58 of its 197 labels at 0.
[RESULT NEEDED: whether the same corrections help on CHO polyreactivity's labels at the floor, against the same move applied to labels not at the floor (Chapter [REF], Section [REF])]
This gives a practical order of work.
Before choosing a method, ask where the labels came from and what shape their noise is likely to have.
Chapter [REF] found that systematic error, a shared offset or a clipped range, does the most damage to a model.
Chapter [REF] found that the same systematic error is the easiest to undo, because it comes with a flag.
Data pooled from several sources or laboratories, assays with a reporting limit, and series measured in batches all carry such a flag.
A method that assumes damage that is not there does harm, though.
Subtracting scaffold-family offsets from Caco-2's labels as delivered took the network's hybrid from 0.2333 to 0.2669 RMSE, because the offsets it removed were real differences between scaffolds.
So the flag must come from how the data were made, not from the method.
This work began with small molecules, and small molecules remain its focus.
The hybrid search, though, takes any set of feature matrices for the same samples and a supervised task, and nothing in it is specific to chemistry.
We ran it on antibodies with the same code and the same search, and on several antibody datasets it worked well.
This was not luck.
The hypothesis behind the hybrid is that the methods were held back by representations whose important features are few and buried among many that carry nothing.
That holds for any domain where several representations describe the same samples.
The adaptive search is what lets the method carry over without being redesigned.
Most antibody representations in use read a language model's embedding of the whole sequence.
We built a set of our own on top of these models.
Several pool the embedding over the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) only, over each CDR separately, or over each of the seven IMGT regions separately.
One takes the change in the embedding from the parent antibody, and another describes each mutation by its residues and the change in hydrophobicity, weight and charge.

Breaking the sequence down by region keeps the parts of the antibody that vary apart from the framework that mostly does not, which is the same problem Chapter [REF] found with general-purpose fingerprints.
Those representations carry the clearest antibody results.
On the anti-VEGF expression scan, the best single representation in hindsight was our CDR readout of ESM3, at 0.7249 Spearman with the SVM, and the hybrid beat it at 0.7729.
On binding free energy, the best single representations were our mutation features with the SVM and the change from the parent embedding with the DNN, at 0.2034 and 0.2215.
The hybrid reached 0.2178 and 0.3542.
We shuffled each representation's features in the binding free energy hybrid in turn.
The representations built for this thesis account for 0.83 of the drop in score with the SVM and 0.68 with the DNN, averaged over the five folds.
On the other antibody datasets they account for between 0.03 and 0.27, so this is where they matter most, not everywhere.
The noise methods also carried over.
On three antibody datasets, cleaning the labels as delivered passed the shuffled-score control, which on small molecules only label smoothing on hERG K_i did by a clear margin.
On SMAC colloidal stability, deletion took the SVM from 0.2740 to 0.4034 Spearman on the single representation and from 0.3108 to 0.3782 on the hybrid.
On binding free energy, label smoothing took the network from 0.3414 to 0.4840, and on expression titer deletion took the random forest's hybrid from 0.2244 to 0.3168.
These datasets were measured in a few experiments on a few hundred antibodies each, and their labels carry real noise that cleaning can find.
The hybrid did not help on every antibody dataset, and the reasons are specific.
On nanobody thermostability, SMAC colloidal stability, HIC retention and CHO polyreactivity it added nothing, for example 0.6899 against 0.6901 Spearman on thermostability with the SVM.
These sets hold a few hundred antibodies, and their held-out folds 35 to 53.
On so few, the search's own scores overstate what the chosen hybrid delivers, by 0.1571 Spearman on colloidal stability with the DNN.
Several of them also carry label problems of their own: thermostability pools five assays into one label, and 58 of CHO polyreactivity's 197 labels sit at the assay floor.
The hybrid needs data, and on the antibody sets with enough of it, or with a representation that sees what varies, it delivered.

Several of the most effective changes in this thesis were the simplest.
Random forests were the most consistent model under label noise across the four datasets of Chapter [REF].

Noise mitigation in molecular data is hard, and for most of this project it did not work.
It works now.
It works best when the data say which labels are wrong, as an assay limit or a scaffold family does.
It works with a detector when the detector is precise enough for the damage at hand.
It works on the labels as delivered too, on hERG K_i and on three antibody datasets, against a control that rules out chance.
Fixing the feature set was the right place to start.
I spent a year on what looked like a separate problem, on the hypothesis that the representation was the root of the trouble with similarity and with noise.
On small molecules the hybrid predicts better than any single representation, gives better neighbors, and keeps its lead through every kind of cleaning.
It carried over to antibodies without redesign, and did best where the representations were built to see what varies.
No single method fits every dataset, and the hybrid does not pretend to be one.
It is a procedure that adapts the features to the data, and it adapts further when the labels are cleaned before it.
A new foundation model appears every few months in molecular, protein and antibody modeling.
With the hybrid search, a researcher does not need to choose between their current representation and a new one.
They add the new embedding to the representations searched and run the search again, and the search decides whether the new embedding contributes features and, if so, how many and which.
A choice usually set by habit or laboratory convention becomes one measured on each task, and it can be measured again every time a new representation appears.
